T(n) \le c \cdot n^2,    \text{for some constant } c > 0
Step 2: Assume the guess is true for $n/2$.
T\left(\frac{n}{2}\right) \le c \cdot \left(\frac{n}{2}\right)^2 = c \cdot \frac{n^2}{4}
Step 3: Substitute into the recurrence.

T(n) \le 2 \left( c \cdot \frac{n^2}{4} \right) + n^2
= \frac{c \cdot n^2}{2} + n^2
Step 4: Check the guess. We want
\frac{c \cdot n^2}{2} + n^2 \le c \cdot n^2
This simplifies to $n^2 \le \dfrac{c \cdot n^2}{2}$, that means $c \ge 2$. So, choosing $c \ge 2$ works.
Step 5: Conclude. So, $T(n) = O(n^2)$. A similar argument gives $T(n) = \Omega(n^2)$. So, $T(n) = \Theta(n^2)$.
Recursion Tree Method

In the recursion tree method, we draw a tree, where the root is the original problem of size $n$, and the children of each node are the smaller recursive calls made by that node. Each node also carries the extra cost $f(n)$ done at that level, not counting its children's cost. We then add up the cost of every level, and add all levels together, to get the total cost.
Step 1: Draw the root. The root is a problem of size $n$, with cost $n$ at that level.
Step 2: Draw the children. The root makes $2$ calls of size $n/2$ each. Level cost is $2 \times \dfrac{n}{2} = n$.
Step 3: Continue expanding. Each of those $2$ nodes makes $2$ calls of size $n/4$. Now $4$ nodes exist, each cost $n/4$, level total $4 \times \dfrac{n}{4} = n$.
Step 4: Notice the pattern. Every level costs exactly $n$, since problem size halves but number of nodes doubles, and these effects cancel.
Step 5: Count the levels. Size goes $n, n/2, n/4, \dots, 1$, giving $\log_2 n$ levels.
Step 6: Total cost.
T(n) = n \times \log_2 n = \Theta(n \log n)
Step 1: Draw the root. Root is size $n$, cost $n$.
Step 2: Draw children. Root makes $3$ calls of size $n/2$. Level cost $3 \times \dfrac{n}{2} = \dfrac{3n}{2}$.
Step 3: Continue expanding. Each of those $3$ nodes makes $3$ calls of size $n/4$, giving $9$ nodes, level cost $9 \times \dfrac{n}{4} = \dfrac{9n}{4}$.

Step 4: Notice the pattern. At level $i$, there are $3^i$ nodes, each of size $n/2^i$, so level cost is $3^i \times \dfrac{n}{2^i} = n \left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^i$. This level cost increases as $i$ increases, since $3/2 > 1$.
Step 5: Count the levels. Number of levels is $\log_2 n$, since size halves every level.
Step 6: Total cost. Since the cost grows with each level, the last level dominates the sum. The last level has $n^{\log_2 3}$ nodes, each doing constant work, giving
T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 3})
which is approximately $\Theta(n^{1.58})$.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Recursion Tree Example 3: $T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/4) + n$

blocks.x: Step 1: Draw the root. Root is size $n$, cost $n$.
Step 2: Draw children. Root makes $2$ calls, one of size $n/2$, one of size $n/4$. Level cost is $\dfrac{n}{2} + \dfrac{n}{4} = \dfrac{3n}{4}$.
Step 3: Continue expanding. The $n/2$ node makes calls of size $n/4$ and $n/8$. The $n/4$ node makes calls of size $n/8$ and $n/16$. Level cost is again less than $n$, around $\dfrac{9n}{16}$.
Step 4: Notice the pattern. Unlike Example 2, here the level cost keeps shrinking, since $\dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4} < 1$. So the root level cost, $n$, dominates the total sum.
Step 5: Total cost. Adding up a shrinking sum across all levels still gives a value close to the root cost, just scaled by a constant. So,
T(n) = \Theta(n)
Extended Master Theorem
The Extended Master Theorem solves recurrences of the form
T(n) = a \cdot T\left(\frac{n}{b}\right) + \Theta(n^k \log^p n)

where $a \ge 1$, $b > 1$, $k \ge 0$ are constants, and $p$ is any real number. Instead of comparing $f(n)$ with $n^{\log_b a}$ directly, we identify the constants $a$, $b$, $k$, $p$, then compare $a$ with $b^k$.
Case 1: If $a > b^k$, the work done by the leaves dominates, then
T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_b a})
Case 2: If $a = b^k$, the work is balanced across all levels, and the log power $p$ decides the answer:
Case 3: If $a < b^k$, the work done at the root dominates, and $p$ decides the answer:
Step 1: Identify constants. $a = 2$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = 0$.
Step 2: Compare $a$ with $b^k$.
a = 2,    b^k = 2^1 = 2    \Rightarrow    a = b^k
Step 3: Apply Case 2, check $p$. Since $p = 0 > -1$, use the first sub-case.
Step 4: Compute the answer.
T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 2} \log^{0+1} n) = \Theta(n \log n)
Step 1: Identify constants. $a = 9$, $b = 3$, $f(n) = n = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = 0$.
Step 2: Compare $a$ with $b^k$.
a = 9,    b^k = 3^1 = 3    \Rightarrow    a > b^k
Step 3: Apply Case 1. The leaves dominate since $a > b^k$.
Step 4: Compute the answer.
T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_3 9}) = \Theta(n^2)

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Extended Master Theorem Example 3: $T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n \log n$

blocks.x: Step 1: Identify constants. $a = 3$, $b = 4$, $f(n) = n\log n = \Theta(n^1 \log^1 n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = 1$.
Step 2: Compare $a$ with $b^k$.
a = 3,    b^k = 4^1 = 4    \Rightarrow    a < b^k
Step 3: Apply Case 3, check $p$. Since $p = 1 \ge 0$, use the first sub-case.
Step 4: Compute the answer.
T(n) = \Theta(n^k \log^p n) = \Theta(n \log n)

blocks.name: Concept
blocks.title: When the Extended Master Theorem Cannot Be Used

blocks.x: The Extended Master Theorem still fails to apply when the recurrence does not fit the exact form $a \cdot T(n/b) + \Theta(n^k \log^p n)$. This happens when $a < 1$, since that is not a valid divide-and-conquer split, or when the subproblem sizes are unequal, like $T(n) = T(n/2) + T(n/3) + n$, or when $f(n)$ is not of the form $n^k \log^p n$ at all, for example $f(n) = 2^n$. In such cases, we go back to the recursion tree method or the Akra-Bazzi method.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: A Case the Basic Master Theorem Missed, Now Solved: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n \log n$

blocks.x: Step 1: Identify constants. $a = 2$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n \log n = \Theta(n^1 \log^1 n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = 1$.
Step 2: Compare $a$ with $b^k$.
a = 2,    b^k = 2^1 = 2    \Rightarrow    a = b^k
Step 3: Apply Case 2, check $p$. Since $p = 1 > -1$, use the first sub-case.
Step 4: Compute the answer.
T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 2} \log^{1+1} n) = \Theta(n \log^2 n)

This is exactly the recurrence that the basic Master Theorem could not solve, since $f(n) = n \log n$ sits exactly on $n^{\log_b a} = n$ with an extra log factor. The extended version handles it directly through the $p$ sub-case.
Solve $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n$ using the Extended Master Theorem.
Solution: $a = 4$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = 0$. $b^k = 2^1 = 2$. Since $a = 4 > b^k = 2$, this is Case 1, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 4}) = \Theta(n^2)$.
Solve $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2$ using the Extended Master Theorem.

Solution: $a = 2$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n^2 = \Theta(n^2 \log^0 n)$, so $k = 2$, $p = 0$. $b^k = 2^2 = 4$. Since $a = 2 < b^k = 4$, this is Case 3, and $p = 0 \ge 0$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n^2 \log^0 n) = \Theta(n^2)$.
Solve $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^2$ using the Extended Master Theorem.
Solution: $a = 8$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n^2 = \Theta(n^2 \log^0 n)$, so $k = 2$, $p = 0$. $b^k = 2^2 = 4$. Since $a = 8 > b^k = 4$, this is Case 1, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 8}) = \Theta(n^3)$.
Solve $T(n) = T(n/2) + n$ using the Extended Master Theorem.

Solution: $a = 1$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = 0$. $b^k = 2^1 = 2$. Since $a = 1 < b^k = 2$, this is Case 3, and $p = 0 \ge 0$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n^1 \log^0 n) = \Theta(n)$.
Solve $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n \log^{-1} n$ using the Extended Master Theorem.

Solution: $a = 4$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = n\log^{-1} n = \Theta(n^1 \log^{-1} n)$, so $k = 1$, $p = -1$. $b^k = 2^1 = 2$. Since $a = 4 > b^k = 2$, this is Case 1, and Case 1 does not depend on $p$ at all, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 4}) = \Theta(n^2)$.

A recursive algorithm is an algorithm that calls itself on a smaller input, until it reaches a base case, which is the simplest input that needs no further recursion. To analyze a recursive algorithm, we first write its recurrence relation, by checking how many recursive calls happen, how much smaller the input becomes, and how much extra work happens outside the calls. Then, we solve this recurrence using substitution, recursion tree, or master theorem, to get the final order of growth.

blocks.name: Concept
blocks.title: General Plan for Recursive Algorithm Analysis

blocks.x: Decide the input size parameter, usually $n$.
Identify the basic operation, the operation that repeats with every call.
Find how many recursive calls are made, and on what smaller size.
Write the recurrence relation, including the base case.
Solve the recurrence to get the order of growth.
Factorial Function

Factorial of $n$, written $n!$, means multiplying all numbers from $n$ down to $1$. The recursive idea is, $n! = n \times (n-1)!$, and the base case is $0! = 1$. So, computing factorial of $n$ depends on computing factorial of $n-1$ first.
Factorial(n)
if n == 0
return 1
else
return n * Factorial(n - 1)
factorial.py
Step 1: Input size. The parameter $n$ is the input size.
Step 2: Basic operation. The multiplication, $n \times \text{Factorial}(n-1)$, is the basic operation.
Step 3: Recursive calls. Each call makes exactly $1$ recursive call, on input size $n-1$.
Step 4: Recurrence relation.
Here, $c$ represents the constant work done outside the recursive call, like the multiplication and the comparison.
Step 5: Solve. Using the recursion tree method, each level reduces $n$ by $1$, and does constant work $c$. The tree has $n+1$ levels, from $n$ down to $0$. Total cost is
T(n) = c \times (n+1) = \Theta(n)
Fibonacci Function

The Fibonacci sequence is $0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, \dots$, where each number is the sum of the two numbers before it. The recursive idea is, $\text{Fib}(n) = \text{Fib}(n-1) + \text{Fib}(n-2)$, with base cases $\text{Fib}(0) = 0$ and $\text{Fib}(1) = 1$. Unlike factorial, here each call makes two recursive calls, not one.
Fibonacci(n)
return n
else
return Fibonacci(n - 1) + Fibonacci(n - 2)
fibonacci.py
Step 1: Input size. The parameter $n$ is the input size.
Step 2: Basic operation. The addition, combining the two recursive results, is the basic operation.
Step 3: Recursive calls. Each call makes $2$ recursive calls, one on $n-1$, one on $n-2$.
Step 4: Recurrence relation.

Step 5: Solve. This recurrence does not fit the Master Theorem, since the two subproblems have different sizes. Using the recursion tree method, each call branches into $2$ more calls, so the tree looks similar to a binary tree, except the depth on the left branch is longer than the right branch. The total number of nodes in this tree can be shown to grow like the Fibonacci numbers themselves, giving
T(n) = \Theta(\phi^n),      \phi \approx 1.618
where $\phi$ is the golden ratio. So, this simple looking function has exponential running time, $\Theta(2^n)$ is also commonly used as a simpler, looser bound for this.
The picture shows the recursion tree for $\text{Fib}(4)$. Notice that $F(2)$ and $F(1)$ are computed many times, again and again, which is the reason this recursion is so slow.
Sum of Digits Function

This function adds up all the digits of a number $n$. The recursive idea is, the sum of digits of $n$ equals the last digit of $n$, plus the sum of digits of the remaining number, after removing the last digit. The base case is, when $n$ becomes $0$, the sum is $0$.
SumOfDigits(n)
if n == 0
return 0
else
return (n mod 10) + SumOfDigits(n / 10)
sum-of-digits.py

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Analysis of Sum of Digits Recursion

blocks.x: Step 1: Input size. Here, the input size is not $n$ itself, but the number of digits in $n$, since each call removes one digit, not one unit. Let us call the number of digits $d$.
Step 2: Basic operation. The addition, $(n \bmod 10) + \text{SumOfDigits}(n/10)$, is the basic operation.
Step 3: Recursive calls. Each call makes exactly $1$ recursive call, on a number with one less digit.
Step 4: Recurrence relation.
Step 5: Solve. Same pattern as factorial, each level does constant work, and there are $d+1$ levels. Total cost is
T(d) = \Theta(d)
Since $d \approx \log_{10} n$, we can also write this as $\Theta(\log n)$, in terms of the value of $n$.
Power Function

This function computes $x^n$, that is $x$ raised to power $n$. There are two ways to write this recursively, a slow way and a fast way. We look at both, to see how the recurrence changes the running time.

blocks.name: Example
blocks.title: Slow Version: One Reduction at a Time

blocks.x: Here, $x^n = x \times x^{n-1}$, with base case $x^0 = 1$.
power-slow.py
Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n-1) + c$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n)$, same pattern as factorial.
Here, we use the idea, $x^n = (x^{n/2})^2$, when $n$ is even, and $x^n = x \times (x^{(n-1)/2})^2$, when $n$ is odd. This way, the power reduces to half each time, instead of reducing by $1$.
PowerFast(x, n)
if n == 0
return 1
else if n is even
half = PowerFast(x, n / 2)
return half * half
else
half = PowerFast(x, (n - 1) / 2)
return x * half * half
power-fast.py
Step 1: Input size. The parameter $n$ is the input size.
Step 2: Basic operation. The multiplication, $half \times half$, is the basic operation.
Step 3: Recursive calls. Each call makes exactly $1$ recursive call, on input size roughly $n/2$.
Step 4: Recurrence relation.

Step 5: Solve using Master Theorem. Here, $a = 1$, $b = 2$, $f(n) = c = \Theta(1) = \Theta(n^0)$. Compute $n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_2 1} = n^0$. Since $f(n)$ matches $n^{\log_b a}$ exactly, this is Case 2, giving
T(n) = \Theta(n^0 \log n) = \Theta(\log n)
This shows the fast version is much better than the slow version, $\Theta(\log n)$ compared to $\Theta(n)$, just by halving the power instead of reducing it by $1$ each time.
A function reverses the digits of a number $n$ recursively, removing one digit and placing it at the end, in each call, until $n$ becomes $0$. Identify the recurrence and find the order of growth.
Solution: Each call reduces the number of digits by $1$, doing constant work. So, $T(d) = T(d-1) + c$, giving $T(d) = \Theta(d) = \Theta(\log n)$.
A function adds up all elements of an array of size $n$, by adding the first element to the sum of the rest of the array, recursively. Identify the recurrence and find the order of growth.
Solution: Each call reduces array size by $1$, doing constant work to add one element. So, $T(n) = T(n-1) + c$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n)$.

The Tower of Hanoi problem moves $n$ disks, by first moving $n-1$ disks to a spare rod, then moving the largest disk, then moving the $n-1$ disks again, on top of it. Identify the recurrence and find the order of growth.

Solution: Each call makes $2$ recursive calls, each on size $n-1$, plus constant work for moving the largest disk. So, $T(n) = 2T(n-1) + c$. Solving by recursion tree, the tree doubles in nodes each level, while the work per node stays constant, giving $T(n) = \Theta(2^n)$.
A function prints numbers from $n$ down to $1$, by printing $n$, then calling itself on $n-1$. Identify the recurrence and find the order of growth.
Solution: Each call reduces $n$ by $1$, doing constant work for the print statement. So, $T(n) = T(n-1) + c$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n)$.

A function computes the GCD of two numbers $a$ and $b$, using $\text{GCD}(a, b) = \text{GCD}(b, a \bmod b)$, until $b$ becomes $0$. This problem is harder to analyze directly using $n$ as size, since the reduction is not a simple halving or minus one, it depends on number theory properties.

Solution: It is known, using a deeper number theory result, that this recursion takes at most $O(\log(\min(a,b)))$ calls, because the smaller number reduces roughly by a multiplicative factor related to the golden ratio, in the worst case, every two calls.
A. Core Logarithm Identities (All logarithms below are base $2$ unless stated otherwise; the base never affects $\Theta$-notation.)
Product rule: $\log(mn) = \log m + \log n$ Example: $\log(8n) = 3 + \log n$.
Quotient rule: $\log(m/n) = \log m - \log n$ Example: $\log(n/4) = \log n - 2$.
Power rule: $\log(n^k) = k \log n$ Example: $\log(n^3) = 3 \log n$.

Change of base: $\log_b n = \dfrac{\log_a n}{\log_a b}$ Example: $\log_2 n = \dfrac{\ln n}{\ln 2}$, so $\log_2 n = \Theta(\ln n)$ – this is exactly why the base of a log is never written inside $\Theta$-notation: changing the base only multiplies by a constant.
Inverse identity: $b^{\log_b n} = n$ Example: $2^{\log_2 n} = n$.
Base facts: $\log_b 1 = 0$, $\log_b b = 1$.

Exponent–log swap (the “hidden” identity): $a^{\log_b c} = c^{\log_b a}$ Example: $n^{\log_2 7} = 7^{\log_2 n}$ – this rewriting is exactly how divide-and-conquer exponents like $\Theta(n^{\log_2 7})$ are manipulated.
The “$n^{1/\log n}$ is a constant” trick: $n^{1/\log_b n} = b$ Example: $n^{1/\log_2 n} = 2$ for every $n$ – a function that looks like it depends on $n$ but is actually $\Theta(1)$.
Sum of logs $=$ log of a factorial: $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log i = \log(n!)$ Example: this identity is the bridge to Stirling's Approximation in Section B below.
For very small x, $\log_{b}(1+x) \approx \frac{x}{\ln(b)}$, where $ln$ is natural logarithm ( base e).

Iterated logarithm $\log^{*} n$: the number of times $\log$ must be applied to $n$ before the result is $\le 1$. It grows slower than $\log\log\cdots\log n$ for any fixed number of iterations. Example: $\log^{*}(65536) = 4$, since $\log\log\log\log(65536) \le 1$; for all practically occurring $n$, $\log^{*} n \le 5$.
B. Factorial and Stirling's Approximation
Stirling's Approximation:
n! = \sqrt{2\pi n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n\left(1 + O\!\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right)   \Longrightarrow   n! = \Theta\!\left(\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n\right)
Example: for $n=10$, Stirling gives $10! \approx 3{,}598{,}696$, versus the true value $3{,}628{,}800$ – accurate to within $1\%$.
Log-factorial form (the single most-used consequence of Stirling):
\ln(n!) = n\ln n - n + O(\log n)   \Longrightarrow   \log(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)
Example: this is precisely why the comparison-based sorting lower bound is $\Omega(n \log n)$, and why $\log(n!)$ and $n \log n$ can always be swapped inside $\Theta$-notation.
Loose factorial bounds (no constants needed):
\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n \;\le\; n! \;\le\; n^n
Example: instantly bounds $n!$ between an exponential and $n^n$ without invoking $\sqrt{2\pi n}$.
Factorial's place in the growth hierarchy: for every constant $c$,
c^n = o(n!)     \text{and}     n! = o(n^n)
Example: $2^n = o(n!)$ and $n! = o(n^n)$, so $2^n \prec n! \prec n^n$.
Central binomial coefficient:
\binom{2n}{n} \sim \frac{4^n}{\sqrt{\pi n}}   \Longrightarrow   \binom{2n}{n} = \Theta\!\left(\frac{4^n}{\sqrt n}\right)
Example: shows $\binom{2n}{n} = O(4^n)$ but $\binom{2n}{n} \ne \Theta(4^n)$ – the $\sqrt n$ factor in the denominator matters.
Sum of all binomial coefficients:
\sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} = 2^n
Example: this is exactly the count of all $2^n$ subsets of an $n$-element set – the standard justification for a Brute-Force paradigm's exponential running time.
C. Summation (Series) Formulas
Arithmetic series:
\sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2)
Sum of squares:
Sum of cubes:
\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^3 = \left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right)^2 = \Theta(n^4)
General power sum:
\sum_{i=1}^{n} i^k = \Theta(n^{k+1}),   \text{for any constant } k \ge 0
Finite geometric series
For $r > 1$: $S_n = \frac{a(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$
For $r < 1$: $S_n = \frac{a(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$
For $S_\infty$ ($|r| < 1$): $S_\infty = \frac{a}{1 - r}$
Harmonic series:
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i} = \ln n + \gamma + O(1/n) = \Theta(\log n),      \gamma \approx 0.5772
Example: directly explains why a loop of the form for(i=1;i<=n;i++) for(j=1;j<=n;j+=i) runs $\Theta(n \log n)$ times in total.
Sum of logarithms:
\sum_{i=1}^{n} \log i = \log(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)
Arithmetico-geometric series ($r > 1$):
\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \, r^i = \Theta(n \, r^n)
Example: $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot 2^i = \Theta(n \cdot 2^n)$ – again dominated by the last (largest-index) term.
Decaying recursion-tree workload:
\sum_{i=0}^{\log n} \frac{n}{2^i} = \Theta(n)
Example: models a divide-and-conquer process where the work per level halves but the number of levels is $\Theta(\log n)$ – the total is still only $\Theta(n)$, not $\Theta(n \log n)$.
Growing recursion-tree workload:
\sum_{i=1}^{\log n} 2^i = \Theta(n)
Example: work doubling every level for $\Theta(\log n)$ levels also sums to only $\Theta(n)$, since the sum is dominated by the final, largest term.
D. Growth-Rate Hierarchy and Limit Tests
Logarithms lose to every polynomial:
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\log n}{n^{\varepsilon}} = 0,   \text{for any constant } \varepsilon > 0
Example: $\log n = o(\sqrt n)$, and even $\log n = o(n^{0.001})$.
Polynomials lose to every exponential:
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{n^{k}}{c^{n}} = 0,   \text{for any constants } k > 0,\ c > 1
The full growth hierarchy (for constants $0<\varepsilon<1$ and $c>1$):
\log^{*} n \;\prec\; \log\log n \;\prec\; \log n \;\prec\; n^{\varepsilon} \;\prec\; n \;\prec\; n\log n \;\prec\; n^{c} \;\prec\; c^{n} \;\prec\; n! \;\prec\; n^{n}
Ratio (limit) test for comparing $f$ and $g$: if $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(n)}{g(n)} = L$, then
0 < L < \infty \Rightarrow f = \Theta(g),      L = 0 \Rightarrow f = o(g),      L = \infty \Rightarrow f = \omega(g)
Example: $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{3n^2+5}{n^2} = 3 \Rightarrow 3n^2+5 = \Theta(n^2)$.
Euler's number limits (used in hashing / amortized / probabilistic analyses):
\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n} = e,      \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n} = \frac{1}{e}
Example: the probability that $n$ items hashed into $n$ buckets avoid a particular bucket entirely is $(1-1/n)^n \approx 1/e$.
Exponential and log inequalities (used to bound the expressions above):
1 + x \le e^{x} \ \text{ for all real } x,      \ln(1+x) \le x \ \text{ for } x > -1
Example: gives the one-line bound $(1 - 1/n)^n \le e^{-1}$ used just above.
E. Floors/ceilings never matter
For a recurrence $T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + f(n)$ with $a \ge 1$, $b > 1$, let $p = \log_b a$.
Floors/ceilings never matter: $T(n) = T(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor) + T(\lceil n/2 \rceil) + O(n)$ has exactly the same solution, $\Theta(n\log n)$, as $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$.
